title: Psalm 116: I Love the LORD, for He Has Heard
summary: A person rescued from the edge of death tells how the ropes of death entangled him, how he called on the name of the LORD, and how God delivered him. He then asks how he can repay such goodness, and answers by lifting the cup of salvation, offering a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and fulfilling his vows before God's people in Jerusalem.
story: Psalm 116 is the fourth psalm of the Egyptian Hallel (113 to 118). Psalm 115 spoke in the voice of the community; Psalm 116 turns to one person who has personally experienced rescue. Placed within the Passover songs, an individual's deliverance from death is set inside Israel's larger story of deliverance from Egypt, so that one believer's thanksgiving becomes part of the whole people's praise. In the order of the Hallel it prepares for the brief call to the nations in Psalm 117 and the great festal thanksgiving of Psalm 118.
historical:
The psalm has no author in its heading. Its language borrows from earlier psalms (verse 3 echoes Psalm 18:4-5, and verse 8 echoes Psalm 56:13), and its Hebrew contains some late features, so many scholars date it after the exile, though it could reflect an older pattern of thanksgiving. The setting is clearly the temple in Jerusalem, where the psalmist fulfills his vows in the courts of the LORD's house. It was likely composed to accompany a thanksgiving offering, and its use at Passover as part of the Hallel came later.

In the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, the psalm is divided into two, with verses 1 to 9 and verses 10 to 19 counted as separate psalms. Paul quotes the Greek form of verse 10, I believed, therefore I spoke, in 2 Corinthians 4:13. The Hebrew of verse 10 is difficult, and translations vary on whether it expresses faith in the midst of affliction or recalls what the psalmist believed and said while suffering.
cultural:
When an Israelite was in danger, he or she often made a vow: a promise to offer a sacrifice or gift to God if rescued. After deliverance, the person went to the temple to pay the vow publicly, usually with a thanksgiving offering, which was a kind of peace offering shared in a meal with family and friends (Leviticus 7:11-16). The psalm is the song of that occasion, told in front of the congregation so that others could hear what God had done.

The cup of salvation in verse 13 was probably a cup of wine poured out as a drink offering or drunk at the thanksgiving meal to celebrate rescue. The phrase son of your maidservant in verse 16 refers to a slave born in the household (compare Exodus 21:4), who belonged to the master from birth and was bound to him more closely than a purchased slave. The psalmist calls himself God's servant in the most complete sense, and yet God has loosed his bonds.
literary: The psalm is an individual song of thanksgiving, with the typical elements: a declaration of love and praise, a narration of distress and deliverance, and a promise to give thanks publicly. It has two halves. Verses 1 to 11 tell the story: the danger (verse 3), the prayer (verse 4), the confession of God's character (verses 5 and 6), and the calm that follows (verse 7). Verses 12 to 19 answer the question “How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?” with public worship. Repeated phrases bind the psalm together: calling on the name of the LORD occurs in verses 4, 13, and 17, and verse 14 is repeated as verse 18. The address to his own soul in verse 7, calling it back to rest, is a notable moment of self-speech.

outline.t: I love the LORD, for he heard me
The ropes of death and a cry for help
What shall I repay? The cup and the vows
Precious death, loosed bonds, and thanks in the temple

doctrines.note: The psalm shows prayer answered: the psalmist called, God inclined his ear, and the result is a lifelong resolve to call on him. Answered prayer leads not to independence but to deeper dependence.

Rescue from death comes from God's grace and compassion, not from the psalmist's strength; he was “helpless, and He saved me.” The fitting response is thanksgiving, not payment, since the only way to repay is to receive more and call on God again.

The psalmist does not hide the anguish, the terror, and the disillusionment of verse 11. Verse 15 adds that the death of God's faithful ones is precious to him, weighty and costly, not something he regards lightly.

words.note: Ahav, to love. The psalm opens with the simple statement “I love the LORD,” a direct declaration of personal love for God that is less common in the Psalms than one might expect. The reason given is concrete: he has heard my voice. Love here grows from experienced mercy.

Sheol, the realm of the dead in Israel's thought, pictured as a place deep below the earth. The anguish of Sheol is the terror of being pulled toward death. The psalmist describes being so close to death that its grip had already seized him.

Yaqar, precious, costly, weighty. When the death of God's saints is precious in his sight, the meaning is not that he is glad when they die but that their death is costly to him and not lightly permitted. The word is used of rare jewels and valuable things.

Todah, thanksgiving, both the song and the sacrifice of thanks. It is the name of the offering the psalmist brings in verse 17. Later Jewish tradition gave the thanksgiving offering special honor, and the word sums up the psalm's response to rescue.

christ: Psalm 116 was sung at Passover as part of the Hallel, and many interpreters think Jesus sang it with his disciples at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30), on the night he was about to face the ropes of death himself. The lifting of the cup and the thanksgiving offering have a natural resonance for Christians with the cup Jesus gave to his disciples as the new covenant in his blood, though the psalm itself does not predict that meal. Paul quotes verse 10 to describe his own ministry, speaking because he believes, in the confidence that the God who raised the Lord Jesus will raise believers too (2 Corinthians 4:13-14). In Christ, the psalmist's rescue from death becomes the believer's hope of resurrection.
questions: The psalmist says he will call on God as long as he lives because God heard him once. What past answer to prayer can strengthen your trust now?
Verse 7 has the psalmist speaking to his own soul. What would you need to say to your own soul to call it back to rest today?
“How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?” How does the psalm's answer differ from the way people usually try to repay a debt?
